details:
**"Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?" (Sonnet 18)**
Shakespeare's most famous sonnet, addressed to the Fair Youth, whom it calls "more lovely and more temperate" than a summer's day. It notes that "rough winds do shake the darling buds of May" and "summer's lease hath all too short a date," and ends by claiming the poem itself will immortalize the youth: "So long lives this, and this gives life to thee." It is the first sonnet after the "procreation" sonnets.

**154 sonnets**
Shakespeare's sonnet sequence, published in a 1609 quarto, contains 154 sonnets. The Shakespearean (English) sonnet form consists of three quatrains followed by a rhyming couplet, in iambic pentameter with the rhyme scheme ABAB CDCD EFEF GG.

**"My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun" (Sonnet 130)**
A Dark Lady sonnet that parodies the conventional blazon of Petrarchan love poetry. The speaker says "coral is far more red than her lips' red," "if snow be white, why then her breasts are dun," "black wires grow on her head," and "music hath a far more pleasing sound," but concludes that his love is as rare as any woman "belied with false compare."

**"Let me not to the marriage of true minds / Admit impediments" (Sonnet 116)**
A sonnet defining true love as unchanging: "Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds." Love is "an ever-fixed mark" and "the star to every wandering bark," and is not "Time's fool" though beauty falls within the compass of Time's "bending sickle." It ends, "If this be error and upon me proved, / I never writ, nor no man ever loved."

**The Fair Youth and the Dark Lady**
The two main addressees of the sonnets. Roughly the first 126 sonnets address a beautiful young man, the Fair Youth, while the later sonnets (127–152) concern the Dark Lady, a dark-haired, dark-complexioned mistress. A Rival Poet who competes for the Youth's patronage appears in a group of sonnets as well.

**The procreation sonnets and Mr. W.H.**
The first 17 sonnets urge the Fair Youth to marry and have children to preserve his beauty, beginning with Sonnet 1, "From fairest creatures we desire increase." Sonnet 2 warns that "forty winters shall besiege thy brow / And dig deep trenches in thy beauty's field." The 1609 quarto was published by "T.T." (Thomas Thorpe) and dedicated to the mysterious "Mr. W.H.," wishing him "that eternity promised by our ever-living poet."

**"That time of year thou mayst in me behold" (Sonnet 73)**
A sonnet in which the aging speaker compares himself to autumn ("bare ruin'd choirs, where late the sweet birds sang"), twilight, and a dying fire. It ends by telling the beloved that seeing this makes "thy love more strong, / To love that well which thou must leave ere long."

**"When to the sessions of sweet silent thought" (Sonnet 30)**
A sonnet in which the speaker "summon[s] up remembrance of things past" and mourns old losses, but concludes that thinking of his friend means "all losses are restored and sorrows end." The phrase "remembrance of things past" became the first English title of Proust's novel.

**Other famous sonnet lines (Sonnets 19, 20, 29, 55, 64, 129)**
Sonnet 19 addresses "Devouring Time," telling it to "blunt thou the lion's paws" and "pluck the keen teeth from the fierce tiger's jaws." Sonnet 20 calls the Youth "the master-mistress of my passion," fueling speculation about Shakespeare's sexuality. Sonnet 29 ends "I scorn to change my state with kings," Sonnet 55 begins "Not marble nor the gilded monuments / Of princes shall outlive this powerful rhyme," Sonnet 64 describes a thought that "cannot choose / But weep to have that which it fears to lose," and Sonnet 129 calls lust "th' expense of spirit in a waste of shame."

**Sonnet 126 (the "envoi")**
The last Fair Youth poem, sometimes called an envoi, is not a true sonnet: it has only twelve lines in rhyming couplets, and the 1609 quarto prints two empty pairs of parentheses where the final couplet would be.

**Narrative poems: Venus and Adonis, The Rape of Lucrece, and "The Phoenix and the Turtle"**
In Venus and Adonis, the goddess of love tries to seduce the young hunter Adonis, who refuses her and is killed by a boar. The Rape of Lucrece describes Tarquin's rape of Lucrece, the wife of Collatine. "The Phoenix and the Turtle" is an allegorical elegy for two lovers who "fled in a mutual flame from hence," ending with a "Threnos" asking the "true or fair" to "sigh a prayer" for the "dead birds."

**Hamlet**
Shakespeare's tragedy about the Danish prince who seeks revenge on his uncle Claudius. It contains the soliloquy beginning "To be, or not to be," which speaks of shuffling off "this mortal coil," and Hamlet's line to Ophelia, "Nymph, in thy orisons / Be all my sins remember'd." Laertes dies poisoned by his own sword, "justly kill'd with mine own treachery." T. S. Eliot coined the term "objective correlative" in his essay on the play.

**The Winter's Tale and other plays**
In The Winter's Tale, Time appears as a chorus to announce a 16-year gap, Antigonus leaves the stage with the famous direction "Exit, pursued by a bear," and a statue of Hermione, the long-dead wife of King Leontes, comes to life. Other clued plays include The Merchant of Venice (Shylock demands a "pound of flesh" from Antonio), Julius Caesar (Mark Antony's "Friends, Romans, countrymen" speech), As You Like It (the "Seven Ages of Man" speech ending in "second childishness"), and the "problem plays" Measure for Measure and Troilus and Cressida.

**Judith Shakespeare (Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own)**
In A Room of One's Own, Woolf imagines that Shakespeare had an equally gifted sister, Judith, who is denied an education (never studying Horace or Virgil), runs away to London to be an actor, becomes pregnant, and kills herself. Woolf uses her to show how society blocked women's creative genius.

**Literary responses and criticism (Greene, Milton, Johnson, Wilde, Shaw)**
Robert Greene's Groats-Worth of Wit attacked Shakespeare as an "upstart Crow" and a "Johannes factotum" with a "Tiger's heart wrapped in a Player's hide." Milton's "On Shakespeare" calls him "Dear son of memory, great heir of fame," Samuel Johnson's Preface praised his characters as "the genuine progeny of common humanity," Oscar Wilde's "The Portrait of Mr. W.H." imagines the sonnets were written for a boy actor named Willie Hughes, and George Bernard Shaw coined "bardolatry." Thomas Bowdler published censored editions of his plays.

**Hamnet, Anne Hathaway, and Ulysses**
Maggie O'Farrell's 2020 novel Hamnet imagines the death of Shakespeare's 11-year-old son from the plague. Carol Ann Duffy's poem "Anne Hathaway" is spoken by his wife, and in Joyce's Ulysses Stephen Dedalus argues that Shakespeare saw himself as the father of Hamlet (the ghost). Modern studies include Harold Bloom's Shakespeare: The Invention of the Human and Stephen Greenblatt's Will in the World.
